issues.legal_issue: A suit should not be rejected for a court-fee shortfall without a fair opportunity to make up the deficiency where the litigant could not pay because of financial difficulty and no mala fides are apparent.
material_facts: The litigant paid only part of the court fee when filing a suit seeking relief concerning his property.
He applied for more time to pay the balance, but the trial court rejected the application and closed the suit without giving him an opportunity to pay.
He said he could not pay because of financial difficulties, and the Court found no manifest ground of mala fides.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s rejection of the suit was wrong and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court discretion to allow a party to make up deficient court fees and to validate the deficiency retrospectively. That discretion should ordinarily be exercised in favour of litigants absent manifest grounds of mala fides, while ensuring bona fides; the court should give an opportunity to pay before rejecting a suit for a fee shortfall.

rule.if: civil_suit and court_fee_shortfall and no_opportunity_to_cure and financial_inability and no_mala_fides_apparent

predicates.civil_suit: A litigant brought a civil suit seeking adjudication of a claim.
predicates.court_fee_shortfall: The litigant paid less than the required court fee when filing the suit.
predicates.no_opportunity_to_cure: The trial court rejected the suit without giving the litigant an opportunity to pay the deficiency.
predicates.financial_inability: The litigant was unable to pay the balance because of financial difficulty.
predicates.no_mala_fides_apparent: The court had no manifest indication that the litigant acted mala fide.

issues.definition: When a civil suit has a fee shortfall, the litigant cannot pay for financial reasons, no mala fides are apparent, and the court gave no chance to cure the shortfall, the rejection is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in paying deficient court fees may be condoned when financial difficulty prevents payment and rejection would prevent adjudication of a substantive claim, consistent with equal access to justice.
material_facts: The litigant could not pay the balance court fee because of financial difficulty, and the suit was rejected on that ground.
The suit concerned the litigant’s substantive claim to property.
The Court considered that the litigant should have an opportunity to have the claim decided on its merits.
issues.conclusion: The delay in payment of the court fee was condoned, and the matter was remanded so the litigant could pay the fee or seek assistance for it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the substantial-justice approach to delay in State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Prasad Singh, Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, and N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy. Article 39A, read with Article 21 and State of Maharashtra v. Manubhai Pragaji Vashi, requires attention to equal access to justice and the effect of economic disability. Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the court to allow deficient court fees to be made up.

rule.if: suit_rejected_for_fee_nonpayment and financial_inability and substantive_claim and no_mala_fides_shown

predicates.suit_rejected_for_fee_nonpayment: A trial court rejected a suit because the litigant had not paid the required court fee.
predicates.financial_inability: The litigant could not pay the required fee because of financial difficulty.
predicates.substantive_claim: The suit sought adjudication of a substantive right rather than merely a procedural advantage.
predicates.no_mala_fides_shown: The record did not show that the litigant’s explanation was mala fide or a dilatory strategy.

issues.definition: When a suit is rejected for nonpayment of fees that the litigant could not afford, the suit concerns a substantive claim, and no mala fides are shown, the delay in payment is condoned.

issues.legal_issue: A litigant who cannot afford court fees may seek legal-services assistance for those fees so that economic disability does not prevent adjudication of the claim.
material_facts: The litigant said that financial constraints prevented him from paying the balance court fee.
The Court noted that eligible persons could receive legal services under the applicable legal-services framework, subject to proof of income.

The Court directed that, if the litigant could not pay, he could apply to the relevant legal-services bodies for assistance with the court-fee amount, and that an application should be considered and facilitated.
issues.conclusion: The litigant was permitted to seek legal-services assistance for the court fee, subject to the applicable eligibility requirements, and the relevant bodies were directed to consider and facilitate such assistance if he applied.
issues.legal_principle: Article 39A, read with Article 21, requires the State to ensure that economic disability does not deny a person access to justice. Section 12(h) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, and Rule 12 of the Kerala State Legal Services Authorities Rules, 1998, provide for legal services for persons meeting the applicable income criteria. The Court relied on State of Maharashtra v. Manubhai Pragaji Vashi.

rule.if: court_fee_required_for_claim and economic_disability and inability_to_pay and income_eligibility_established and legal_aid_application_made

predicates.court_fee_required_for_claim: A litigant had to pay court fees to have a claim adjudicated.
predicates.economic_disability: The litigant faced financial hardship affecting access to the court.
predicates.inability_to_pay: The litigant could not pay the required court fees.
predicates.income_eligibility_established: The litigant established that the applicable income eligibility requirements were met.
predicates.legal_aid_application_made: The litigant applied to the relevant legal-services body for assistance with the court fees.

issues.definition: When a litigant needing court fees cannot afford them, meets the applicable income criteria, and applies for assistance, the request for court-fee assistance is to be considered and facilitated.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in appealing the rejection of a suit may be condoned when the litigant was unaware of the rejection and acted after learning of it, with an acceptable explanation for the delay.
material_facts: The litigant appealed the rejection of his suit and sought condonation of delay.
He said he did not know that the trial court had rejected the suit and believed his request for more time to pay court fees would be allowed.
After learning from his advocate that the suit had been rejected, he applied for a certified copy that same day.
The High Court rejected the condonation application for lack of sufficient grounds, but the Supreme Court found that decision unsustainable.
issues.conclusion: The delay in filing the appeal before the High Court was condoned.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act permits condonation where sufficient cause is shown. The Court applied the substantial-justice and pragmatic approach in State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Prasad Singh, Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, and N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy, and relied on Muneesh Devi v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. Length of delay is not by itself decisive; the acceptability of the explanation is the criterion.

rule.if: appeal_from_suit_rejection and litigant_unaware_of_rejection and prompt_action_after_learning and acceptable_explanation

predicates.appeal_from_suit_rejection: The litigant sought to appeal the rejection of a suit.
predicates.litigant_unaware_of_rejection: The litigant did not know that the trial court had rejected the suit.
predicates.prompt_action_after_learning: After learning of the rejection, the litigant promptly took steps to obtain the decision and pursue an appeal.
predicates.acceptable_explanation: The litigant gave an explanation for the delay that the court accepted.

issues.definition: When a litigant appealing a suit’s rejection was unaware of it, acted promptly after learning of it, and gave an acceptable explanation, the appeal delay is condoned.
